keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The page names Dongping (modern Heze), Langye (modern Linyi) and Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) in Shandong, with 'eight prefectures' in support in 621 and no list; the page does not mention the Huai, Jiangsu or Anhui. Three 70 km circles are the researcher's reading; no frontier is on the page.

ledger.note: 617: Xu Yuanlang rises against the Sui. 'By spring 617' he had captured Dongping and expanded to Langye with more than 20,000 men (infobox reign 617-623). The page gives no month; 'by spring 617' is an upper bound.

region.text: Dongping (modern Heze), Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) and Langye (modern Linyi): the three places the Xu Yuanlang page names in Shandong

ledger.note: 621: Xu submits to the Tang. After Dou Jiande fell and Wang Shichong surrendered, Xu submitted to Tang, 'was made the commandant of Yan Prefecture' and was again named Duke of Lu, so his land is the Tang's until he rises with Liu Heita later in 621 (the next event, which gains it back from the Tang). Added by reviewer ea-04-x so that the 621 gain follows a loss; the Tang ledger has no mirror for either.

region.text: Dongping (modern Heze), Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) and Langye (modern Linyi): the three places the Xu Yuanlang page names in Shandong

ledger.note: 621: eight prefectures rise with Xu. After Liu Heita rose against the Tang in 621, Xu 'rises, captures the Tang general Sheng Yanshi' and gains 'support from eight prefectures'; the prefectures are not named, so the land is the three-circle reading.

621: Xu Yuanlang declares himself Prince of Lu. 'Winter 621: Xu declares himself Prince of Lu', after holding the nominal Tang title Duke of Lu (given again in 621 when he submitted and became commandant of Yan Prefecture).

region.text: Dongping (modern Heze), Yan Prefecture (modern Jining) and Langye (modern Linyi): the three places the Xu Yuanlang page names in Shandong

ledger.note: 622: Tang armies attack Xu. After Li Shimin defeated Liu Heita in summer 622, 'Li Shentong, Li Shiji, and Ren Gui keep attacking his territory'; no town or date of capture is on the page, so the zone is the three-circle reading.

ledger.note: 623: the contest ends with the siege of Yan. In spring 623 Tang forces besieged Xu's capital at Yan, 'his soldiers surrendered in large numbers' and Xu was killed by local men (infobox 26 March 623).

ledger.note: 623: Xu Yuanlang is killed and Tang takes the territory. He 'fled with a few guards and was killed by men in the countryside' on 26 March 623 (infobox); footnotes cite a February 623 date (Zizhi Tongjian) and a 624 date (Old Book of Tang).

sources.title: Xu Yuanlang
sources.note: Rise by spring 617 at Dongping and Langye, the nominal submissions of 618-621, the 621 rising with eight prefectures, Prince of Lu in winter 621, the 623 siege of Yan and death on 26 March 623.

notes: Written for ea-04-x (listed by ea-03-f as 'Xu Yuanlang (Lu)'; no Cliopatria row). One page only (Xu_Yuanlang); the page names no area and no frontier, so the three Shandong circles are a reading. Open points: (1) the page gives Xu's nominal submissions to Li Mi (spring 618), Yang Tong and the Tang (619, Duke of Lu), Wang Shichong's Zheng (619), Dou Jiande's Xia (winter 619) and the Tang again (621), which belong in those suzerains' ledgers as vassal pairs if at all (all were nominal); the Tang, Sui, Xia, Zheng and Li Mi dossiers have no mirror; (2) the date of death is 26 March 623 in the infobox and February 623 / 624 in footnotes; the year 623 is the one used; (3) Yucheng (modern Shangqiu, Henan) is on the page but its link to Xu is not given; (4) Xu's land was part of Dou Jiande's Xia sphere in 619-621, which the Xia dossier may draw as its own. Gazetteer: Heze, Jining and Linyi (Shandong) are places; 'Dongping', 'Langye' and 'Yan Prefecture' are not names in the gazetteer.
